title: Given a Scenario, Deploy and Configure Multifunction Devices, Printers, and Settings

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Deploying a printer or multifunction device requires correct physical setup, software, connectivity, sharing, settings, security, network scanning, and scanner hardware.
sections.callout: PLACE → INSTALL → CONNECT → SHARE → CONFIGURE → SECURE → SCAN

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes deployment, a connection method, a driver issue, a print setting, a security requirement, or a scan destination, identify which layer of printer configuration is being tested.
bullets: PCL vs. PostScript → printer language and driver choice
Identity before job release → authentication and secured print

sections.title: Properly Unboxing the Device
paragraphs: Before powering on a new printer or multifunction device, remove protective tape, foam, shipping locks, cartridge restraints, scanner locks, and internal packing material.
sections.callout: New printer makes unusual mechanical noises → check for unremoved shipping material.

sections.title: Choosing the Setup Location
paragraphs: Choose a location with sufficient space, ventilation, power, network access, wireless signal, user accessibility, paper handling, and maintenance clearance. Avoid unsuitable heat and moisture conditions.
bullets: Leave room to open paper trays and scanner lids.
Preserve access to side panels, toner compartments, and maintenance doors.
Confirm wired or wireless connectivity at the selected location.
sections.callout: Place the device where it can operate and be serviced safely.

sections.title: Operating-System Printer Drivers
paragraphs: A printer driver translates between the operating system, applications, and printer. Use a driver that matches the printer model, operating system, and OS architecture when relevant.
sections.callout: Printer is detected but features are missing or output is wrong → verify the driver.

sections.title: Printer Control Language (PCL)
paragraphs: Printer Control Language (PCL) is widely supported and commonly associated with efficient general-purpose office and business printing.
sections.callout: Standard office documents → PCL may be appropriate.

sections.title: PostScript
paragraphs: PostScript is a page-description language known for precise text and graphics rendering. It is associated with publishing, design, graphics, and consistent page output across platforms.
sections.callout: Graphics-heavy document requiring page fidelity → PostScript.

sections.title: PCL vs. PostScript
sections.callout: OFFICE → PCL. GRAPHICS/PAGE FIDELITY → POSTSCRIPT.

sections.title: Printer Firmware
paragraphs: Printer firmware is software stored on the device that controls its hardware and internal functions. Updates can fix bugs, improve compatibility, address security vulnerabilities, and add features.
sections.callout: Driver = software on the computer. Firmware = software inside the printer.

sections.title: Device Connectivity
paragraphs: Printers can connect through USB, Ethernet, or wireless networking. Select the connection based on whether the device serves one computer or network users.
sections.callout: Identify whether the printer is local, wired-networked, or wireless-networked.

sections.title: USB Printer Connectivity
paragraphs: USB commonly provides a direct local connection between one computer and a printer.
sections.callout: One desktop directly connected to a printer → USB.

sections.title: Ethernet Printer Connectivity
paragraphs: Ethernet connects a printer directly to a wired network and is well suited to stable shared printing in office environments.
sections.callout: Printer available directly on the wired LAN → Ethernet.

sections.title: Wireless Printer Connectivity
paragraphs: Wireless connectivity places a compatible printer on the network without an Ethernet cable. Confirm signal strength, network coverage, security, and credentials.
sections.callout: Network printing without a network cable → wireless.

sections.title: USB vs. Ethernet vs. Wireless
sections.callout: ONE COMPUTER → USB. NETWORK CABLE → ETHERNET. NO NETWORK CABLE → WIRELESS.

sections.title: Public/Shared Devices
paragraphs: A printer serving multiple users can be exposed through a printer share or managed centrally by a print server.
sections.callout: Determine whether the need is simple sharing or centralized management.

sections.title: Printer Share
paragraphs: A printer share makes a printer attached to or configured on one computer available to other users.
sections.callout: Printer connected to PC A but needed by other PCs → printer share.

sections.title: Print Server
paragraphs: A print server centrally manages printers and print jobs. It can manage queues, deploy drivers, enforce access control, and administer multiple printers.
sections.callout: Many shared printers managed from one central system → print server.

sections.title: Printer Share vs. Print Server

table.caption: Shared-printing models
rows: Queues, drivers, access, and multiple printers

sections.callout: SHARE = expose a printer. SERVER = centrally manage printing.

sections.title: Configuration Settings
paragraphs: Common printer configuration settings include duplex, orientation, tray settings, and print quality.
sections.callout: Match the requested output behavior to the exact setting.

sections.title: Duplex Printing
paragraphs: Duplex printing places output on both sides of the paper.
sections.callout: Reduce paper use by printing both sides → duplex.

sections.title: Page Orientation
paragraphs: Orientation controls page direction. Portrait is taller than wide; landscape is wider than tall.
sections.callout: Wide spreadsheet → try landscape orientation.

sections.title: Tray Settings
paragraphs: Tray settings identify the paper size, paper type, and source tray. Examples include Letter, Legal, labels, envelopes, and specialty paper.
sections.callout: Printer requests a different paper size despite loaded paper → check tray settings.

sections.title: Print Quality
paragraphs: Print-quality settings control resolution, draft or high-quality output, and toner or ink usage. Higher quality can increase print time and consumable use.
sections.callout: Quality balances output appearance against time and resources.

sections.title: Printer Security
paragraphs: Shared printers and multifunction devices can process sensitive information. Objective 3.7 includes user authentication, badging, audit logs, and secured prints.
sections.callout: Protect device access, job release, and activity records.

sections.title: User Authentication
paragraphs: User authentication requires a person to prove identity before accessing printer functions.
sections.callout: Only authorized employees may use the device → user authentication.

sections.title: Badging
paragraphs: Badging lets a user authenticate by presenting an identification badge or card to the device.
sections.callout: Employee taps a company badge before printing → badging.

sections.title: Audit Logs
paragraphs: Audit logs record printer activity such as who used the device, when the activity occurred, and other security-related events.
sections.callout: Security team needs printer-usage history → audit logs.

sections.title: Secured Prints
paragraphs: A secured print job remains held until the authorized user releases it, preventing sensitive output from sitting unattended in a tray.
sections.callout: Confidential document waits for the employee → secured print.

sections.title: Authentication vs. Secured Print

table.caption: Identity and job-release controls
rows: Holds the job for authorized release

sections.callout: Authentication and secured printing often work together.

sections.title: Network Scan Services
paragraphs: A multifunction device can send scanned documents directly to email, a Server Message Block (SMB) network share, or a supported cloud service.
sections.callout: Identify the requested destination: mailbox, shared folder, or online service.

sections.title: Scan to Email
paragraphs: Scan to email creates a digital document and sends it to an email destination, commonly as an attachment.
sections.callout: Scanned document delivered directly to an inbox → email.

sections.title: Scan to SMB
paragraphs: Server Message Block (SMB) allows the multifunction device to save a scanned file to a network shared folder.
sections.callout: Scan directly into a departmental network folder → SMB.

sections.title: Scan to Cloud Services
paragraphs: A multifunction device can upload scanned documents directly to supported cloud storage or another online service.
sections.callout: Scan directly to an online storage destination → cloud service.

sections.title: Email vs. SMB vs. Cloud Scanning
sections.callout: INBOX → EMAIL. SHARED FOLDER → SMB. ONLINE STORAGE → CLOUD.

sections.title: Automatic Document Feeder (ADF)
paragraphs: An Automatic Document Feeder (ADF) pulls multiple loose pages through the scanner for batch scanning or copying.
sections.callout: Scan a 30-page loose document automatically → ADF.

sections.title: Flatbed Scanner
paragraphs: A flatbed scanner captures an item placed on glass. It is suited to single pages, photographs, books, fragile originals, and items that should not pass through rollers.
sections.callout: Scan a bound book or delicate photograph → flatbed.

sections.title: ADF/Flatbed Scanner

table.caption: Scanner input methods
rows: Books, photos, fragile or single items

sections.callout: STACK → ADF. GLASS → FLATBED.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Shipping locks or tape → proper unboxing
Ventilation, access, and network availability → setup location
Printer exposed through another computer → printer share
Paper source, size, or type → tray settings
Hold job for user → secured print
Book or photo on glass → flatbed

sections.title: Objective 3.7 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Printer deployment scenarios mix drivers, connections, sharing, settings, security, scanning, and scanner hardware. Identify the layer the scenario actually tests.

entries.title: Driver vs. Firmware
paragraphs: A driver runs in the operating system; firmware runs inside the printer.

entries.title: PCL vs. PostScript
paragraphs: PCL fits general office printing; PostScript emphasizes precise graphics and page-description rendering.

entries.title: USB vs. Ethernet
paragraphs: USB is a direct local connection. Ethernet places the device directly on the network.

entries.title: Printer Share vs. Print Server
paragraphs: A host can share one printer; a print server provides centralized infrastructure and management.

entries.title: Duplex vs. Orientation
paragraphs: Duplex controls paper sides; orientation controls page direction.

entries.title: Tray vs. Quality
paragraphs: Tray settings identify paper source, size, and type. Quality controls appearance, resolution, and resource use.

entries.title: Authentication vs. Audit Log
paragraphs: Authentication controls access; an audit log records activity.

entries.title: Authentication vs. Secured Print
paragraphs: Authentication verifies identity; secured print holds the job for authorized release.

entries.title: ADF vs. Flatbed
paragraphs: ADF handles a stack of loose pages; a flatbed scans an item placed on glass.

sections.title: Printer Deployment Workflow
bullets: PLACE: unbox correctly and select a safe, serviceable location.
INSTALL: use the correct OS driver and printer firmware.
CONNECT: choose USB, Ethernet, or wireless.
SHARE: configure a printer share or print server when required.
CONFIGURE: set duplex, orientation, trays, and quality.
SECURE: apply authentication, badging, audit logs, and secured prints.
SCAN: configure email, SMB, or cloud destinations and choose ADF or flatbed input.
sections.callout: PLACE → INSTALL → CONNECT → SHARE → CONFIGURE → SECURE → SCAN
